title: Artificial intelligence in undergraduate medical education: an updated scoping review
extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI), especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, has been used in undergraduate medical education (UGME) and how the literature changed after the public release of generative AI tools in late 2022. The authors aimed to map the evolving landscape of AI-related publications, identify major application areas, summarize perceptions of AI among students and faculty, and clarify what competencies, teaching methods, and ethical considerations are being proposed for medical curricula.

The study is a scoping review conducted with Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards. The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, Google Scholar, and Unika for English- and Spanish-language publications from January 2020 to April 2024. After screening 3,238 records, they included 310 publications covering medical students, faculty, and UGME-related AI applications. The review synthesized studies on autonomous tutoring, personalized learning, simulation, assessment generation and grading, feedback tools, and LLM performance on exams and educational tasks.

The review found rapid growth in AI-related UGME literature after ChatGPT’s release, with most studies reporting positive attitudes toward AI but also concerns about accuracy, bias, plagiarism, and overreliance. The authors conclude that evidence remains early and fragmented, with many studies small, single-site, and focused on perceptions or short-term outcomes rather than robust learning effects. They argue for clearer AI competencies, longitudinal curricular integration, faculty development, and stronger evaluation of impacts on critical thinking, clinical reasoning, ethics, and assessment practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for conversational text generation, question answering, tutoring-style support, and content creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied across multiple UGME uses including personalized learning, exam preparation, generating learning content and exam questions, self-assessment, case-based learning support, and feedback/assessment tasks; also discussed as the most frequently mentioned LLM-based tool in the review.

findings.finding_summary: Across the included UGME literature, ChatGPT was reported as helpful for exam preparation, clarifying complex physiological processes, creating mnemonics, explaining clinical vignettes, and generating learning content. It was also found useful for medical terminology learning and case-based learning support, though the review notes content-quality and accuracy concerns and emphasizes the need for human oversight.
findings.measure: Reported usefulness, posttest scores, and qualitative evaluations of learning support and content accuracy across included studies

findings.finding_summary: The review summarized several studies in which ChatGPT performed at or near passing levels on USMLE exams and was compared with other tools for question answering. However, other included studies reported it was unreliable for some self-assessment tasks and that outputs sometimes contained inaccuracies, especially when used to generate exam questions or answer long-form questions.
findings.measure: Exam performance, self-assessment performance, and accuracy on generated/answered questions

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot/LLM system, including Bard/Gemini-family tools, used for conversational assistance and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned in a comparison study summarized in the review as being used alongside ChatGPT for answering multiple-choice and long-answer medical questions.

findings.finding_summary: In the review’s summary of included studies, Bard (normalized here to Gemini) was compared with ChatGPT on medical question answering. ChatGPT was slightly superior on endocrinology and diabetes MCQs, while both models lacked up-to-date information; another study found ChatGPT-3.5 and Bard unreliable as self-assessment tools for medical studies.
findings.measure: Multiple-choice question answering and self-assessment reliability

quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review synthesizing heterogeneous studies rather than a single controlled experiment or meta-analysis. The evidence is broad but mostly descriptive, with many included studies being surveys, perspectives, or small interventions.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports potentially meaningful educational uses of ChatGPT and Gemini-family tools, but the effect magnitude is largely not reported and many findings are qualitative or mixed. Reported impacts appear promising but remain uncertain and context-dependent.
